title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive 11 days after he quit; shares jump 31%
dek: The board said it acted after input from senior levels of the US government and found no national security risk. Congressional hearings are due next week.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Nvidia, the company whose chips power most of the world's artificial intelligence systems, reinstated Jensen Huang as president, chief executive and board member on Monday, with immediate effect, 11 days after he resigned. Its shares rose about 31 per cent, their third-best day on record, according to reports, lifting the wider US market after a sharp sell-off in technology stocks last week.

In a release filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Nvidia said its board had acted unanimously after discussions with Mr Huang and after receiving input from senior levels of the United States government, and had concluded that his return poses no national security risk. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA," said Harvey C. Jones, the board chair. "I am honored to return to NVIDIA," Mr Huang said.

## A reversal in a week

Mr Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, resigned on 12 November after reports that US intelligence officials had concerns about a person close to him whom they suspected of gathering information for China. Beijing called the allegation a smear. On 17 November Mr Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate him.

The company's release says an independent committee of directors, advised by outside counsel, is still investigating reports that Mr Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, and that he supports the inquiry. The board has also set up a National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks, and is hiring a chief compliance officer. Colette Kress, who served as interim chief executive, stays on as chief financial officer.

## What they are saying

President Donald Trump said he had spoken "directly and indirectly" with the board, called Mr Huang a "national treasure" and said he "did nothing wrong", according to reports. Attorney General Todd Blanche reportedly told the president the Justice Department had no evidence of wrongdoing by Mr Huang or Nvidia.

Not everyone was persuaded. "No national security risk? Based on what?" asked Senator John Cornyn, a Texas Republican. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, called the decision "reckless" and asked for more openness about Mr Trump's role, reports said. California's attorney general's office said it would continue looking into whether Nvidia misled investors.

## Why it matters

Nvidia sits at the centre of the US-China contest over AI chips. Washington now requires licences for advanced chips sent to foreign data centres that serve Chinese firms, and a House committee has published documents showing approvals for hundreds of thousands of chips for Chinese companies. Any doubt over the company's leadership feeds straight into that debate, and into the plans of countries such as India that rely on Nvidia processors for national AI computing programmes.

## What happens next

Mr Huang is due to sit for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December, and Nvidia's general counsel is to appear before them on 2 December, according to reports. Mr Huang is scheduled to testify in public before the Senate Banking Committee on 3 December.
